Amelia Earhart expedition heads to Pacific atoll hoping to find her plane

Reuters

10 October, 2026 04:00 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Steve Gorman LOS ANGELES, Oct 10 (Reuters) – A US-based team of marine archaeologists has set sail for a tiny island in the far western Pacific seeking to examine the latest tantalizing clue to one of the 20th century’s great unsolved mysteries: the 1937 disappearance of famed aviator Amelia Earhart.

Backed by Purdue University, an institution long affiliated with Earhart and her legacy, the group aims to learn whether a submerged object detected by satellite imagery in the island’s lagoon six years ago is the wreckage of Earhart’s twin-engine Lockheed Electra 10-E airplane.

Such a finding would conclusively prove the hypothesis of some scholars that Earhart and her navigator, Fred Noonan, crash-landed on or near the coral-ringed atoll and perished as castaways there, hundreds of miles from their intended refueling stop.

Show Full Article

After embarking from Los Angeles earlier this month, the group was expected to arrive on Tuesday, October 13, local time at Nikumaroro, an uninhabited speck of land in the remote Phoenix Islands, part of the archipelago nation of the Kiribati Republic.

“Finding Amelia Earhart’s Electra aircraft would be the discovery of a lifetime,” Richard Pettigrew, head of the Archaeological Legacy Institute in Eugene, Oregon, who is leading the effort in conjunction with Purdue, said in press materials for the mission.

Purdue general counsel and expedition member Steve Schultz, who was in Fiji conducting advance work for the expedition last week, said in an interview: “This would be solving one of the great mysteries in aviation history, certainly one of the great mysteries of the 20th century,”

The mission has its skeptics. Chief among them is rival Earhart explorer Ric Gillespie, co-founder of TIGHAR, short for The International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, and author of the 2024 “One More Good Flight: The Amelia Earhart Tragedy.”

TREE OR PLANE?

Gillespie has led a dozen expeditions of his own to the atoll over three decades and is the leading proponent of the Nikumaroro castaway theory. But he predicted the Pettigrew-Purdue team would find no airplane wreckage or anything else of consequence left on the island.

The Purdue team credits Gillespie for laying the foundation of the theory they hope to prove. And they cite a compelling body of evidence that he has amassed over the years, including human artifacts recovered on the island, such as a 1930s-era glass cosmetic jar for freckle cream and remnants of a jackknife like one Earhart carried on the plane.

Gillespie’s investigation also encompassed modern forensic analysis from records of measurements of skeletal remains found on the island in the 1940s; logs of radio transmission bearings from distress calls picked up by wireless operators in the days immediately after Earhart vanished; and a photograph taken of the island’s shoreline months later showing an object that Gillespie said appears to be the Electra’s landing gear.

In a Reuters interview last week, Gillespie said he believes the plane has since been lost to history, eventually swept by tides off the coral flat where it had landed largely intact and carried into the sea to sink and break apart in the surf.

Two previous attempts to locate the plane’s wreckage in the surrounding ocean, including a 2019 operation conducted by marine archaeologist Robert Ballard, famed for his discovery of the wreck of the Titanic, proved fruitless, Gillespie said.

A plane-shaped sonar image from elsewhere on the sea floor turned out to be a pile of rocks.

“I’d love to find that airplane. It ain’t gonna happen,” Gillespie said.

Pettigrew and his team are betting otherwise. To them, the multi-branched shape first noticed in a 2020 satellite image resembles an aircraft fuselage and wings. They assert that the object, or part of it, has since been spotted in earlier aerial images of the island’s lagoon dating as far back as 1938.

Gillespie said he is certain that the object in question was actually a fallen pandanus tree, a palm-like evergreen native to the island region, that washed into the lagoon.

“You can see the root ball. You can see the branches,” Gillespie said in the interview. “It’s a tree. People see what they want to see.”

‘GAS IS RUNNING LOW’

The official US government view has long been that the Electra ran out of fuel and crashed at sea near its refueling destination of Howland Island, another dot of land about 400 miles northwest of Nikumaroro, then known as Gardner Island.

Earhart was last seen taking off in her Electra on July 2, 1937, from Papua New Guinea en route to Gardner, about 2,500 miles (4,000 km) to the east, during a multi-stage attempt to become the first woman to pilot a plane around the world.

Definitive radio contact with the plane was lost the next day after Earhart, 39, reported “gas is running low,” followed by her final known transmission giving her geographical line of position.

The disappearance spawned the largest US government search ever undertaken for a lost aircraft, including a flyover of Gardner, but no trace of the Electra or its crew was found at the time.

The $900,000 Purdue mission, consisting of 17 people, plans to remain on Nikumaroro for five days before making the six-day return boat trip to the Kiribati capital, Tarawa, according to Schultz.

Purdue, based in West Lafayette, Indiana, would ultimately seek to bring back any bits of the Lockheed Electra that might be recovered.

Earhart was essentially a visiting faculty member at Purdue for two years as a women’s career counselor and advisor to the school’s aeronautics department. A Purdue research grant paid for development of the Electra, which she called her “flying laboratory.”

Purdue lawyer Schultz said if the plane were found, no artifacts would be removed from it on this trip. Any effort to extract the aircraft wreckage would require further permission from the Kiribati government, he said.

(Reporting by Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Editing by Jonathan Spicer )

Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after Florida landfall, NHC says

Reuters

10 October, 2026 01:00 pm IST

Follow Us :

By Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Pardesi Oct 10 (Reuters) – Isaias weakened to a post-tropical cyclone on Saturday, having rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast as a Category 2 hurricane, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, the US National Hurricane Center said in its latest advisory.

The post-tropical cyclone, crossing over southern Alabama after making landfall earlier near Destin, Florida is about 55 miles (89 km) south-southwest of Montgomery, Alabama, with maximum sustained winds of 65 mph (100 kmh), the agency added.

Isaias is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland before weakening below gale force later on Saturday, the NHC said.

Show Full Article

The center warned of possible storm surges, urban and river flooding and flash floods across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.

A risk for tornadoes will also persist overnight across the Florida Panhandle and north Florida into southern Georgia, while the tornado threat will continue on Saturday across parts of the Florida Panhandle, Georgia, and the Carolinas, the agency said.

Alabama’s emergency management agency said the hurricane has downed trees and power lines, making travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning.

“Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice,” it posted on X. “These road closures will remain in effect until conditions are deemed safe for travel.”

President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations, told reporters outside the White House, “We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” adding that it was “under control.”

More than 430,000 people in Florida and nearly 297,000 in Alabama lost power as the storm hit shore, according to power outage tracking firm PowerOutage.us.

“Emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.

Florida’s emergency services urged residents to shelter in place and watch for hurricane conditions across the north of the state.

(Reporting by Rhea Rose Abraham and Rajveer Singh Pardesi in Bengaluru; Editing by William Mallard and Ros Russell)

Pressure mounts on India poll chief Gyanesh Kumar over voter list changes

Reuters

10 October, 2026 11:00 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

By Saurabh Sharma NEW DELHI, Oct 10(Reuters) – India’s “Cockroach” youth movement and opposition parties are pushing hard for election chief Gyanesh Kumar to resign over accusations of widespread manipulation of voter lists during an exercise to verify one billion voters.

The calls come a month after US President Donald Trump praised the former bureaucrat, who took over as India’s chief election commissioner in February 2025, for insisting that voters prove their identity with photo ID, unlike in the US.

Criticism of Kumar, who has denied all accusations, soared last month after a report in the Indian Express newspaper.

Show Full Article

The paper said his two deputies had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions regarding voter rolls, registration procedures and the poll body’s digital systems.

Election Commission data shows that more than 130 million names, a figure exceeding the population of Japan, have been struck off the voter list since the latest round of revisions began last year.

Nearly 650 million people of the 960 million registered voted in the last general election in 2024.

The opposition has long claimed that the government is trying to fix voter lists to its advantage and was quick to repeat the accusations after the Indian Express report.

Government ministers, Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party and the poll body have all denied the charges.

Kumar, 62, and the two other election commissioners have not commented, but the Election Commission said, “Differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution”.

PROTEST THREAT

The youth-led Cockroach Janta Party has called a protest in New Delhi on Saturday to demand Kumar’s resignation, and the main opposition alliance led by the Congress party has also staged protests this week calling for him to step down.

Kumar has defended the actions of the poll body and told a press conference last year: “For the Election Commission, there is neither an opposition nor a ruling side; everyone is equal.”

When Trump praised him, Kumar was riding high in sections of the Indian media last month. But since the Indian Express report, graffiti have appeared near his ancestral home in northern India calling him a traitor.

Kumar joined the Indian Administrative Service in 1988 after completing his B.Tech in civil engineering from an elite government college in his northern home state of Uttar Pradesh.

He previously worked in the defence and home ministries, and retired in January 2024. Two months later he was appointed an

election commissioner, before eventually becoming the chief.

Kumar has had a troubled relationship with opposition parties from the start of his tenure as chief. Opposition lawmakers presented a motion in parliament for his removal this year, but it was rejected.

(Reporting by Saurabh Sharma in New Delhi; Editing by Alexandra Hudson and Clarence Fernandez)
